tip: In Brazil the object pronoun goes before the verb: pode me ajudar (can you help me), not 'ajudar-me' as in Portugal.
todo + a singular noun with no article means every: todo verão (every summer). Add the article, todo o verão, and it means the whole summer.
Quem (who) as a subject always takes a singular verb: quem cozinhou, even if more than one person might have cooked.
Emotion adjectives take com for the thing that caused them: surpreso com a notícia (surprised by the news), where English uses by or at.
To take a class or course, Portuguese uses fazer (to do), not 'tomar': fazendo um curso = taking a course.
Regular -er verbs in the past drop -er and add -eu for he/she/you: comer becomes comeu (ate).
After a feeling noun, use de before the verb: vergonha de falar (embarrassed to speak), medo de cair (afraid to fall).
de + o contracts to do: típico do Nordeste (typical of the Northeast). You cannot keep them apart as 'de o.'
Por que in two words asks a question; porque in one word means because: Por que o preço subiu?
pronto para + an infinitive means ready to do something: pronto para sair (ready to leave).
In Brazil você (you) pairs with te for the object: quem te contou (who told you), mixing você with the older te.
acabar means to run out, and the thing that ends is the subject: o dinheiro acabou (lit. the money ran out), not 'I ran out.'
vamos + an infinitive is how you say let's: vamos fazer alguma coisa (let's do something).
mais before an adverb makes the comparative: mais cedo (earlier), mais tarde (later).
mudar de + a noun means to switch something: mudou de emprego (changed jobs), mudar de ideia (change your mind).
acontecer (to happen) is used only in the third person: o que aconteceu? (what happened?), isso acontece (that happens).
In the past, conhecer means to meet for the first time: conheceu = met. In the present it means to know.
In Brazil esse and essa often mean this, not just that: essa carreira = this career.
começar a + an infinitive means to start doing something: começou a trabalhar (started working).
A they-form verb with no stated subject means they or someone in general: não me avisaram = they didn't tell me.
gostar always needs de before the thing you like: gostaram do restaurante (liked the restaurant), never gostar it directly.
Que + an adjective or noun means how or what a: que chato (how annoying), que legal (how cool).
